newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers fight to stop flood "catastrophe".
newsitem.headline: German soldiers fight to stop flood "catastrophe".

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers on Friday fought to reinforce a sodden dike protecting a swathe of low-lying land from the swollen Oder river as authorities ordered a mass evacuation of the area.
Further south, water submerged two villages after dikes holding back the Oder burst in two places -- bringing to eastern Germany flooding that has already battered other parts of central Europe.

About 1,500 border guards were helping the emergency operation with 65 helicopters and 100 boats, and a further 5,400 soldiers were in the region to help out -- the German army's largest peacetime operation since World War Two.

Officials said it would be catastrophic if dikes gave way in the Oderbruch region north of Frankfurt an der Oder, a low-lying area which was drained and turned into farmland 250 years ago and protected from the Oder by man-made dikes.
"We have no idea when this catastrophe will be over," Manfred Stolpe, premier of Brandenburg state told a news conference, calling the flooding the worst to hit the region in over a thousand years.
"Don't underestimate the danger or be deceived by the slow pace of the climb of the water. It is climbing slowly, slowly, but it is still climbing," he said.

Bernd Vollbort, a regional official, said if a dike burst at Hohenwutzen, at the north of the Oderbruch, 250 square kilometres of land could be under water within a few hours and a fifth of the town of Bad Freienwalde could be submerged.
A spokesman for the region's crisis centre said 1,000 helpers were working to try to stop the dike bursting.
"The sheer force of nature being kept at bay is huge," Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told German radio.
But state interior minister Alwin Ziel held out hope for the area. "The heart of the Oderbruch is hanging on this (dike)," said Ziel. "But we still have a chance."

Fire sirens and church bells were sounded in the Oderbruch and local television broadcast messages warning 5,000 residents in around 17 villages to start evacuation after officials decided the Hohenwutzen dike could give way.
Trucks carrying sheep and cattle rolled out of the area, the bread basket of the former communist East Germany -- a fertile plain growing grains, vegetables and sunflowers.
Authorities estimate up to 19,000 of the Oderbruch's 20,000 inhabitants could have to be evacuated if the dike burst.

South of Frankfurt an der Oder, officials said about 3,000 people in the villages of Ziltendorf and Wiesenau would have to leave as a result of the second breach, south of another dike which burst on Wednesday.
Officials said evacuations in both areas were progressing slowly as some residents were reluctant to follow orders and leave their homes, belongings and livestock.
"As long as there is no water here, noboby is leaving," said one man in the village of Zaeckericker Loose in the Oderbruch area. But he had loaded his car just in case.

Germany has so far has escaped the worst of the region's flooding -- the most serious in centuries -- which claimed more than 100 lives and inundated thousands of homes earlier this month in the neighbouring Czech Republic and Poland.
